paras: The lynching of Henry Cook took place on the night of Sunday, November 11, 1888, in the swamps of Miller County, Georgia, where a group of men ran him down and killed him. Cook had been accused of breaking into a widow's home while drunk and assaulting her 12-year-old daughter. The killing was known only through a short dispatch from Bainbridge, Georgia, which ran in a few papers in Tennessee, Kentucky and Florida.

According to the Bainbridge dispatch, Cook lived below Cheevertown in Baker County. The dispatch said he went in an intoxicated condition to the home of a widow named Jones in Miller County and behaved so that the family hid from him. Her daughter, aged twelve, shut herself in a room and barricaded the door while the others took refuge outside in the dark. Cook was accused of breaking down the door and assaulting the girl; the papers stated the charge as fact, and no arrest or court proceeding preceded his death.

Once the alleged assault became known, a party of men hunted Cook through the swamps. The fuller version of the dispatch, printed by the Quincy Herald, said he was lynched by "25 or 30 masked men" who "made short work of him" as soon as they caught him. Neither version names any of the men, states Cook's race, or describes how he was killed.
No report of an inquest, arrest or other official response appears in the coverage.

The Clarksville Evening Chronicle in Tennessee printed the story on November 14 under a Bainbridge dateline of that day and the headline "Lynched for Outraging a Child." The Evening Bulletin of Maysville, Kentucky, ran the identical text and headline the same day among its wire briefs. On November 17 the Quincy Herald in Florida carried a longer, unheadlined paragraph credited to a Bainbridge dispatch dated November 12, which added the number of men, their masks and Cook's home in Baker County. All three accounts presented the accusation as established and said nothing about the lawfulness of the killing.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Cook
bases: Henry Cook was reported 'lynched' in Miller county, Ga., by men, 25 or 30 of them masked by one version, who hunted him down in the swamps after an accusation of assaulting a child (A1, A3).

Cook was reported lynched without any legal process by 'men' (A1), given as 25 or 30 masked men (A3), who pursued him after he was accused of criminally assaulting a 12-year-old girl, which meets the standard definition; all of this rests on one Bainbridge dispatch.
A1 and A3 are versions of the same Bainbridge, Ga., dispatch (A2 reprints A1 word for word), and no independent local account, inquest or follow-up was found.

accounts.label: Bainbridge wire report
accounts.gist: Cook went drunk to the Jones home, broke into the room where the 12-year-old daughter had barricaded herself and 'outraged her person'; he was lynched Sunday night by men who ran him down in the swamps.

accounts.label: Bainbridge dispatch (Quincy Herald version)
accounts.gist: The same dispatch, dated Nov. 12, adds that 25 or 30 masked men did the killing, that Cook lived in Baker county, and that once the assault was made known the men hunted him down and 'made short work of him.'

framing.detail: Ran the short Bainbridge wire under the headline 'Lynched for Outraging a Child', treating the accusation as fact with no comment on the lynching.
Ran a fuller, unheadlined paragraph attributed to 'A dispatch from Bainbridge'; it stated the accusation as fact and said the men 'made short work of him'.

conflicts.note: Both versions put the lynching on Sunday night, Nov. 11; only the dateline differs, and the Nov. 14 dateline in A1 may be the wire's date of transmission.
